analysis.one_liner: Bans mandatory arbitration and class-action waivers in employee retirement and benefit plans.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in May 2022 with no cosponsors, referred to the Senate labor committee, and died there without a hearing or vote when the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend the federal law governing employer-sponsored retirement and benefit plans (ERISA) to make forced arbitration clauses, class-action waivers, and waivers of representation unenforceable, and would bar plans from including them. It would also stop plans from writing in 'discretionary clauses' that make it much harder for a worker to win a benefits lawsuit in court, requiring courts to review benefit denials fresh rather than deferring to the plan's own decision. The bill never advanced past its referral to the Senate committee that handles labor matters.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and retirees in employer-sponsored retirement, health, and other benefit plans who want to sue over denied benefits or plan mismanagement. Under current law, plans can force those disputes into arbitration and bar class actions, which leaves individual workers with claims too small to litigate alone and no way to pool them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers and retirees with benefit disputes

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes predispute arbitration clauses in employee benefit plans unenforceable, so a participant could take a benefits dispute to court instead of a private arbitrator.
It bars class-action waivers and representation waivers, letting plan participants join together in class or collective claims over plan benefits.

It outlaws discretionary clauses, which currently let plans give themselves final say over benefit decisions and force courts to defer to those decisions; the bill would require courts to review benefit determinations from scratch (de novo).

A post-dispute arbitration agreement would remain possible, but only if the participant got plain-language notice, at least 45 days to consider it, and gave written consent without any coercion, and a court rather than an arbitrator would decide any dispute over the clause's validity.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that sponsor benefit plans, and the companies and people hired to run them, would lose their ability to channel benefits lawsuits into arbitration, block class actions, and shield their benefit decisions from meaningful court review. Benefit disputes would be more likely to be litigated in court, and class actions over plan mismanagement would become viable again.

drawbacks.text: Employers and plan administrators argue that arbitration resolves disputes faster and more cheaply than court, and that allowing class actions and fresh judicial review of benefit decisions would raise litigation costs and could discourage employers from offering generous voluntary benefits.
The bill applies to new disputes as of enactment even before plan documents are updated, so plans and participants could face a transition period of legal uncertainty over which provisions govern.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the benefit is direct: ERISA claims are often small individually, and forced arbitration plus class-action waivers has effectively erased many of them. The cost falls on plan sponsors and administrators in the form of more court litigation, and some of that cost could be passed back through benefit administration. The arbitration-avoidance provisions are broadly structured (courts decide enforceability, arbitration only by informed written consent after a dispute), though the immediate effective date creates some transition uncertainty.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, where it sat with no cosponsors, no hearing, and no vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Tina Smith introduced the bill on May 12, 2022, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee.
No other senator cosponsored the bill.
No further action was taken after the committee referral; the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that sponsor benefit plans and the administrators who run them keep the current system, under which benefit disputes can be forced into arbitration, class actions can be waived, and courts defer to the plan's own benefit decisions. Workers with benefits disputes remain in that system.

for.name: Tina Smith
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its sole sponsor; no senator joined as a cosponsor.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee leadership
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Patty Murray (D-WA)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or committee vote on the bill, leaving it unacted on after referral for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no partisan split is recorded; it was sponsored by one Democrat with zero cosponsors from either party.

industries.note: The bill would strip plans of forced arbitration, class-action waivers, and discretionary clauses, exposing employers to benefit lawsuits they can currently avoid. Workers would gain enforceable recourse against denied or mismanaged benefits.

industries.industry: Benefits plan administrators and service providers
industries.note: Administrators currently benefit from discretionary clauses that force courts to defer to their benefit decisions; the bill would require fresh judicial review and would bar covered people from imposing arbitration on participants.

industries.industry: Arbitration providers and defense-side employment law firms
industries.note: Mandatory arbitration in benefits disputes is a source of demand for arbitration services and for firms defending plans in arbitration; the bill would eliminate that stream for benefits claims.

industries.industry: Employee-benefit plaintiffs' firms and plan participants
industries.note: With class-action waivers unenforceable, class and collective claims over plan benefits would become possible again, creating work for firms representing workers and real recourse for participants.
